sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
A nanostructured Ag/In/Cu foam is prepared by a facile electrochemical method and evaluated as a catalyst for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. The electrodeposited In is partially displaced by Ag to investigate the catalytic CO-producing activity of Ag/In catalyst with different composition of Ag and In, which is easily controlled by adjusting the displacement time of Ag. In order to provide a large electrochemical surface area, we then employ bubbletemplated Cu foam as a roughened metal support for the Ag/In catalyst. The Ag/In/Cu foam catalyst exhibits notable performance to other previous catalysts, in terms of CO Faradaic efficiency and partial current density, especially in low overpotential region. The result is ascribed to the suppressed hydrogen evolution by In and morphological advantage by Cu foam.
Keywords: electrochemical CO2 reduction; carbon monoxide; electrocatalyst; nanostructure

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
To cope with the increased emission of greenhouse gas and the global climate change, various efforts have been conducted [1,2]. Among them, an electrochemical conversion of CO2 has received significant attention because it produces high-value fuels and the feedstocks for C1 chemistry, such as CO [3-18], HCOOH [19,20], CH3OH [21,22], and CH4 [23,24], at room temperature and ambient pressure. The process is completely clean and complements the unsustainability of conventional energy sources if electricity from renewable sources is used for this conversion [25]. Among the various products, the CO produced from the electrochemical conversion of CO2 has many advantages [26-28]. As a major component of syngas, CO has high economic value because it can be used to produce value-added hydrocarbons in various industries [26]. In addition, this conversion process requires only two electrons [27,28]. However, the high stability of CO2 leads to a large overpotential for its activation; consequently the development of a highly active electrocatalyst is essential to resolve this problem [29,30]. High selectivity is also required for CO2 reduction because competitive proton reduction occurs in aqueous solutions where the CO2 is dissolved [31].
Among various metal electrocatalysts for the production of CO, Ag is a strong candidate considering its activity, selectivity, and price [32]. Recent studies of Ag and Ag-based electrocatalysts have focused on controlling morphology and composition [8-18]. As representative studies on the control of Ag morphology, nanoporous Ag [8], Ag corals [9], Ag inverse opals [10], and Ag dendrites [11] have been reported. With various morphologies of controlled roughness and crystal structure, the enhanced CO Faradic efficiencies and partial current densities were obtained [8-11]. Meanwhile, Ag-based bimetallic catalysts have been developed by alloying various transition metals such as Cu [12,13], In [14,15], Zn [16], and Sn

[17], demonstrating that a composition has a significant effect on the CO Faradaic efficiency and partial current density. In addition, the morphologies of Ag-based bimetallic catalysts can also be controlled by adjusting their compositions (e.g., Ag-Cu and Ag-In dendrites) [12,14]. However, these methods are still disadvantageous in terms of catalyst utilization because they require large amounts of loaded Ag to form three-dimensional nanostructures, which means that the active catalytic sites in the bulk cannot be utilized because the electrochemical CO2 reduction mostly occurs on the surface of the catalyst.
In our recent study, we reported the facile preparation of a Ag/Cu foam catalyst using bubbleassisted Cu electrodeposition following Ag displacement [33,34]. Due to the morphological advantages of a highly roughened surface, the Ag/Cu foam exhibited high CO partial current densities over the −0.5 to −0.9 VRHE (RHE: reversible hydrogen electrode) potential range. However, a compositional disadvantage originating from partially exposed Cu at the surface resulted in poor CO Faradaic efficiencies at more negative potentials. As a strategy to solve the problem, a transition metal having poor hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity should be selected as the support for the Ag catalyst. Due to the unoptimized H-chemisorption energies, thereby having large overpotential for the HER, several transition metals, such as In, Sn, Bi, and Pb, could suppress the hydrogen evolution at highly negative potentials where the electrochemical CO2 reduction occurs [35]. In addition, their lower standard reduction potentials facilitate the spontaneous displacement by Ag, which should enable us to fabricate the catalyst at room temperature and ambient pressure [36].
In the present study, various Ag/In catalysts were prepared by successive In electrodeposition and Ag displacement for the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO. Ag coverage and the surface composition of the Ag/In catalyst increased with Ag displacement time, and were

In order to further improve catalytic performance, bubble-assisted Cu foam (CF) was employed to provide a large electrochemical surface area (ECSA) for the Ag/In catalyst. Compared with the reported values, the Ag/In/CF catalyst exhibited enhanced or comparable CO Faradaic efficiencies and partial current densities.

sections.heading: 2.1. Fabrication of the Ag/In and Ag/In/CF catalysts
sections.text:
A laboratory-made Teflon cell was used to construct a conventional three-electrode cell system for In electrodeposition. The working electrode was pretreated as follows. Commercial In foil (Alfa Aesar, area: 1 cm × 1 cm, thickness: 0.127 mm) was immersed in 30% ethanol solution for 2 min to remove organic materials, after which the native oxide of the In foil was removed by dipping the foil in 0.1 M HCl for 2 min. The exposed area of the working electrode was 0.44 cm2. Pt wire and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) were used as the counter and reference electrodes, respectively. Prior to any electrochemical process, all electrolytes were purged with N2 gas (99.995%) for 30 min. The In electrodeposition electrolyte contained 10 mM InCl3·H2O (99.99%, Alfa Aesar) and 500 mM HClO4 (60%, Duksan). Galvanostatic electrodeposition was performed at −1000 mA/cm2 for 1800 s, controlled by a potentiostat (Autolab PGSTAT 302 N, Metrohm). Ag displacement was then carried out at room temperature in an electrolyte composed of 10 mM AgNO3 (99.9%, Alfa Aesar) and 10 mM 2-nitrobenzoic acid (95%, Sigma Aldrich) [37]. Ag displacement times of 60, 300, 600, and 1200 s were employed.
Bubble-templated CF electrodeposition was performed on commercial Ti foil (Sejin, 2 cm × 2 cm, thickness: 0.1 mm) following the procedure described in our previous study [33,34]. The electrodeposited CF was immersed in 0.1 M H2SO4 for 300 s in order to remove native oxides from the Cu surface [38]. The In electrodeposition was performed on the CF at −50 mA/cm2 for 900 s followed by Ag displacement for 600 s for the preparation of Ag/In/CF.

sections.heading: 3.1. Fabrication and characterization of the Ag/In catalysts
sections.text:
Prior to Ag displacement, In was electrodeposited onto commercial In foil (Figure 1a) at a constant deposition current of −1000 mA/cm2 for 1800 s in an electrolyte composed of 10 mM InCl3 and 500 mM HClO4 (Figure 1b). Micrometer-scale polygonal shapes were obtained that exhibited continuous morphologies with numerous holes, consistent with literature reports [39]. The In deposits were then immersed in an electrolyte composed of 10 mM AgNO3 and 10 mM 2- nitrobenzoic acid. Due to the different standard reduction potentials (In3+/In0: −0.34 VNHE and Ag+/Ag0: +0.79 VNHE), Ag displacement occurred spontaneously [36]. We introduce the following nomenclature for the prepared catalysts: “Ag#/In”, where “#” refers to the Ag displacement time (s). In the FESEM image of Ag60/In (Figure 1c), a number of Ag particles are observed to be sparsely formed on the surfaces of the In polygons. The Ag-particle density and coverage continued to increase with displacement time, to 300 s (Ag300/In, Figure 1d) and 600 s (Ag600/In, Figure 1e). Exposed In was barely visible, but still existed in the Ag600/In sample, as shown in the inset of Figure 1e. A further increase in Ag displacement time to 1200 s led to morphological changes that resulted in hierarchical nanoplates with high coverage over the surfaces of the In polygons (Figure 1f).
Figure 2 displays compositional analyses of the Ag#/In samples. The EDS elemental maps reveal that Ag is well distributed on the surfaces of the electrodeposited In polygons in each sample. The Ag composition of Ag60/In was 11.5%, which increased to 21.8% in Ag300/In, to 42.6% in Ag600/In, and to 63.8% in Ag1200/In. The overlaid EDS maps include both In and Ag and reveal gradual color changes from cyan (In) to gray (Ag) with increasing Ag displacement time.

Figure 3a demonstrates linear sweep voltammograms of commercial In foil, electrodeposited In, and the Ag#/In samples, at a scan rate of 10 mV/s in the N2-purged 0.1 M KOH electrolyte. Anodic peaks were observed near −0.12 VRHE for the commercial In foil and the electrodeposited In, which correspond to the oxidation of In metal to the hydroxide [40]. Following Ag displacement, anodic currents for Ag oxidation were observed in the 1.2–1.8 VRHE potential range. The first anodic peak corresponds to the formation of Ag2O (2Ag + 2OH − ↔ Ag2O + H2O + 2e−). The further positive sweeping revealed an oxidation of Ag2O to AgO (Ag2O + 2OH − ↔ 2AgO + H2O + 2e −) [41]. With increasing Ag displacement time, the anodic current recorded at potentials greater than 1.2 VRHE continuously increased, reflecting that the surface became Agrich as evidenced in Figure 2. Although the Ag oxidation current increased, no significant change in the In oxidation peak current was observed, which is ascribed to poor mass transfer of Ag ions from the bulk electrolyte to the interior of the In during Ag displacement. Figure 3b displays the XRD patterns of commercial In foil, electrodeposited In, and the Ag#/In samples. All peaks were normalized by the intensity of the In(110) peak at 39.2°. For commercial In foil, peaks corresponding to metallic In were observed at 33.0° (101), 36.3° (002), 39.2° (110), 54.5° (112), 56.6° (200), 63.2° (103), 67.0° (211), and 77.0° (004), consistent with its tetragonal crystal structure [JCPDS #05-0642]. After In electrodeposition, the normalized intensities of the In(112), In(200), and In(103) peaks were observed to decrease. After displacement by Ag, the normalized intensity of the Ag(111) peak observed at 38.1° increased with increasing Ag displacement time. The Ag1200/In sample, which exhibited Ag nanoplates (Figure 1f), displayed obvious Ag(200) and Ag(220) peaks at 44.3° and 64.4°, respectively, in its XRD pattern. Further increases in the surface Ag composition to 91.1% (Ag1200/In) resulted in a slightly lower CO Faradaic efficiency of 40.5%. The maximized CO Faradaic efficiency at the specific Ag composition in Ag-In bimetallic catalyst have previously been reported, showing the enhanced HER suppression by In content [14]. As a reference, the Ag commercial foil showed CO Faradaic efficiency of 18.4% at the low bias potential. Figure 4b displays CO Faradaic efficiencies over the −0.33 to −0.73 VRHE potential range. The CO Faradaic efficiencies were lower than 17.1% for the commercial In foil over the entire potential range. The CO Faradaic efficiency was enhanced following In electrodeposition on the In foil, exhibiting values of 25.1–36.2%. This improvement might be related to changes in roughness and crystal structure, as it has been observed for other metallic catalysts [10,18]. The CO Faradaic efficiency of the Ag600/In catalyst in the lower overpotential region (−0.33 to −0.43 VRHE) was enhanced by ~20%, whereas the values in the higher overpotential region (−0.53 to −0.73 VRHE) were mostly similar to those of the electrodeposited In. It seemed that Ag600/In behaved like In-catalyst in this region, where the catalyst is known to be active toward HCOO– production [15]. In order to confirm this, other products were also analyzed over all potential ranges (Figure 4c). As a liquid product of Ag600/In catalysis, the Faradaic efficiency for the formation of HCOO– was determined to be 10.0 and 17.3% at −0.63 and −0.73 VRHE, respectively. It should be noted that the HER is still suppressed at these potentials. In addition, it has been reported that further shift of potential to negative direction for In@Ag catalyst increased the production of HCOO– and H2 [15]. sections.heading: 3.3. Fabrication and characterization of the Ag/In/CF catalyst
sections.text:
In order to provide a more roughened support for the Ag600/In catalyst, a CF structure was fabricated by bubble-templated Cu electrodeposition on a Ti substrate (Figure 5a) as shown in Figure 5b. The pore size, wall thickness, and surface morphology of CF are in good agreement with previous results [33,34]. In electrodeposition was then performed on the CF in an electrolyte composed of 10 mM InCl3 and 500 mM HClO4 at a constant deposition current of −50 mA/cm2 for 900 s (In/CF, Figure 5c). The surface morphology of the In/CF was dramatically different to the pristine CF, exhibiting slightly thicker walls consistent with the formation of In on the outer walls of the Cu substrate. The In/CF sample was immersed in an electrolyte composed of 10 mM AgNO3 and 10 mM 2-nitrobenzoic acid for 600 s (Ag600/In/CF, Figure 5d) [37]. The walls were observed to be thinner following Ag displacement, and several particles formed on the outer-wall surfaces.
Compositional analysis of the Ag600/In/CF sample was conducted by EDS elemental mapping of which the result is shown in Figure 6. Strong Cu signals were obtained inside the pores (Figure 6a), whereas strong In signals were locally detected at the outer walls (Figure 6b), confirming that In was selectively electrodeposited on the surfaces of the outer Cu walls of the foam structure. Similar maps were obtained for Ag because the difference in the standard reduction potential between Ag and In is much larger than that between Ag and Cu (Figure 6c). A further possible reason for this observation involves the slower mass transfer of Ag ions from the bulk electrolyte to the insides of the pores; several brighter regions indicate the presence of

agglomerated Ag on the surfaces of the outer walls. We conclude that Ag displacement occurred efficiently at the outer walls rather than within the pores.
The CF, In/CF, and Ag600/In/CF samples were electrochemically characterized by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in a N2-purged 0.1 M KOH electrolyte at a scan rate of 1 mV/s (Figure 7a). For CF, the peak observed at 0.56 VRHE is consistent with Cu oxidation in the alkaline electrolyte (2Cu + 2OH- → Cu2O + H2O + 2e -) [41]. As the potential is swept in the positive direction, two anodic peaks are observed, consistent with further oxidation of Cu2O [41]. Following In electrodeposition (In/CF), the anodic peaks previously observed for the oxidations of Cu and Cu2O were absent that reflected a high coverage of In on CF. Moreover, an anodic peak was observed near −0.12 VRHE, consistent with the oxidation of In metal to the hydroxide [40]. Following Ag displacement (Ag600/In/CF), the current density of the In oxidation peak was observed to decrease and a weak anodic current was observed near 1.62 VRHE, consistent with the formation of Ag2O [41]. It should be noted that an anodic peak at 1.25 VRHE may be assigned to either Cu or Ag oxidation (or both), because the potentials for their oxidations overlap. The XPS spectra of Ag600/In/CF support this hypothesis, as shown in Figures 7b. The weak but obvious Cu 2p peaks were detected along with strong In 3d and Ag 3d signals. Given that, we could assume that some of the In beneath the Cu could have dissolved during the Ag displacement process, leaving a small portion of Cu exposed at the surface. Still, it was believed that the oxidation was relatively more weighted on Ag, considering that Ag resided in the outmost layer of the catalyst. The EDS reveals that the compositions of Cu, In, and Ag in the bulk of the Ag600/In/CF sample are 55.2%, 36.6%, and 8.2%, respectively. On the other hand, XPS reveals that the composition of Cu at the surface is significantly lower, at 9.2%, whereas that of surface Ag is dramatically higher, at 52.2%. sections.heading: 3.4. Catalytic activities of Ag/In/CF for electrochemical reduction of CO2
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2-conversion experiments were conducted on the Ag600/In/CF catalyst, then the results are compared with Ag300/In and Ag600/In catalysts. As shown in Figure 8a, the Ag600/In/CF catalyst exhibited higher CO Faradaic efficiencies at all potentials. In the relatively low overpotential region of −0.33 to −0.43 VRHE, the CO Faradaic efficiencies of Ag600/In/CF were slightly higher than those of Ag300/In and Ag600/In. However, at −0.53 VRHE, the Ag600/In/CF showed much higher CO Faradaic efficiencies; a maximum value of 77.4% was observed. At the potential, the much smaller charge transfer resistance of Ag600/In/CF was obtained compared with that of Ag600/In (Figure S5). Then, the CO Faradaic efficiencies were gradually decreased as the potential was negatively shifted. Although the surface Ag/In ratio of 1.35 in Ag600/In/CF catalyst was similar with that of 1.32 in Ag300/In catalyst, the enhanced CO Faradaic efficiency demonstrated the morphological advantage provided by the CF support. The foamy support not only provided the large ECSA to the catalyst, but also probably affected the mass transport of CO2 near the electrode surface as speculated in other studies [42,43], In specific, the open-cell foam structure would accompany a pressure-drop inside pores and cause a mass-transfer limitation of CO2. Along with the limited mass transfer, poor buffering inside the

However, the fact that Ag600/In/CF catalyst outperformed Ag300/In and Ag600/In catalysts in CO2/CO Faradaic efficiency indicated that the large ECSA more dominantly contributed in improving the catalytic activity and in determining selectivity. Furthermore, relatively high concentration of electrolyte in the present study should minimize the difference of bulk and local pH, which resolves the potential problem of affecting the Faradaic efficiency. In addition, the employment of In in Ag/In/CF effectively inhibited hydrogen evolution, and thus the local pH should be maintained as same as the bulk, especially in low-overpotential region. For the Ag300/In and Ag600/In catalysts, the decrease of CO Faradaic efficiency in the higher overpotential region could be explained by the HCOO– production in the presence of In (Figure 4c) [15]. Accompanying with this effect, for Ag600/In/CF catalyst, the exposed Cu surface (9.2 %) contributed to accelerate the HER [44], resulting high H2 Faradaic efficiency of 33.9% at −0.73 VRHE. It was noteworthy that the total Faradaic efficiency from Ag600/In/CF in Figure 8a did not reach 100%, and this was ascribed to the aforementioned Cu exposure. Cu converts CO2 to other chemical species, such as HCHO or CH3OH than CO, especially in low- and mid-biased potential region. Even with small portion of Cu exposed in Ag600/In/CF catalyst, the chemicals could be generated on the surface of Cu, thereby presenting the total Faradaic efficiency lower than 100%. In short, Ag was the main catalytic component contributing the conversion of CO/CO2. In passivated HER and participated in the conversion of HCOO -/CO2. Finally, Cu seemed to affect the formation of C1 species from CO2, but its portion is very small. As shown in Figure 8b, the Ag600/In/CF catalyst exhibited superior CO partial current densities, originated from high CO selectivity and larger ECSA. In addition, stability test of Ag600/In/CF was conducted at a constant potential of −0.53 VRHE as shown in Figure S6a. The CO Faradaic

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: A nanostructured Ag/In/CF catalyst was electrochemically prepared by a facile fabrication method at room temperature and ambient pressure. The controlled Ag displacement facilitated to obtain high CO Faradaic efficiency at a specific surface composition where the HER suppression was maximized. As a cost-effective support, the CF provided a large ECSA for the Ag/In catalyst, which enhanced the CO-production rate. Compared with reported activities, notable performance was observed for Ag600/In/CF in terms of CO Faradaic efficiency and partial current density, especially in the low overpotential region.
